calls.head: Top line on top line: McDavid vs. Kakko
calls.body: At home, the Oilers keep sending McDavid’s line (Nugent-Hopkins, McDavid and Kapanen) out against opponents’ first lines, far more often than chance would suggest. Mike Babcock has been choosing strength on strength. Tonight the Kraken’s first line is Kakko, Beniers and Samoskevich.

calls.nums: At home: 63% of this group’s 5-on-5 time against first lines, about 44% with no line matching

With no line matching, this group would face first lines about 44% of the time, about as often as those lines are on the ice.

calls.said: Mike Babcock would send Nugent-Hopkins, McDavid and Kapanen out against the Kraken’s first line again

calls.head: The Kraken can’t afford to take penalties
calls.body: The Kraken’s penalty kill is one of the league’s worst, and the Oilers’ power play is one of the best. Discipline matters more than usual for the Kraken tonight. Edmonton has had one of the league’s most effective power plays for years.

calls.head: Depth vs. star power
calls.body: On depth, Seattle is near the top of the league, but Edmonton is the worst. They’re about as far apart as two teams get. If this one comes down to the bottom six, that suits the Kraken.

EDM.head: We gave Edmonton a 64% chance, but Seattle had other ideas.

SEA.head: We gave Seattle only a 36% chance, and they proved us wrong.

surprises.head: Edmonton brought the hits
surprises.body: Edmonton usually hits more than most teams. Even by those standards, this was a lot of hitting: a hit score of 212 in the close stretches of the game, against their usual 110 (100 is league average, adjusted for the arena’s scorer). A team strays this far about once every 175 games. That’s rarer than once a season for any one team.

surprises.head: Edmonton’s shots went from harmless to more harmless
surprises.body: Edmonton usually gets some of the league’s least dangerous shots, and Seattle is one of the league’s best at preventing dangerous shots. Even by those standards, this was a night of harmless shots: Edmonton’s shots at 5-on-5 had a 2.9% chance of scoring on the average shot, against their usual 5.9% (about 5.5% against Seattle) and a league average of 6.4%. A team strays this far about once every 80 games.

story.head: Kakko has two goals as the Kraken hold off the Oilers
paras: Jordan Eberle struck first for the Kraken midway through the first, but Connor McDavid tied it 1-1 for Edmonton on the power play early in the second. Leon Draisaitl gave the Oilers the lead midway through the period, and that was all they would get. Joey Daccord took over from Philipp Grubauer in net for Seattle to start the third, after two goals against. Kaapo Kakko tied it 2-2 for Seattle with a little over seven minutes left. He struck again with a little over five minutes left to put the Kraken ahead for good. Vince Dunn sealed it into the empty net with less than two minutes left.
Nothing much separated these two on the chances. This one could have gone either way. The Oilers hit two posts and the crossbar and still lost. Tristan Jarry stopped 27 of 30 for the Oilers.

The officials called 14 penalties, a total the league sees about once every 40 games. The Kraken moved to 12-10-1 and climbed to fourth in the Pacific, while the Oilers dropped to 17-7-4, still first in the Pacific.
